name: Appleman and a Sheet of Paper
description: Appleman has a very big sheet of paper. This sheet has a form of rectangle with dimensions 1 × n . Your task is help Appleman with folding of such a sheet. Actually, you need to perform q queries. Each query will have one of the following types: Fold the sheet of paper at position p i . After this query the leftmost part of the paper with dimensions 1 × p i must be above the rightmost part of the paper with dimensions 1 × ([ current width of sheet ] - p i ) . Count what is the total width of the paper pieces, if we will make two described later cuts and consider only the pieces between the cuts. We will make one cut at distance l i from the left border of the current sheet of paper and the other at distance r i from the left border of the current sheet of paper. Please look at the explanation of the first test example for better understanding of the problem.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers: n and q ( 1  ≤ n ≤ 10 5 ; 1 ≤ q ≤ 10 5 ) — the width of the paper and the number of queries. Each of the following q lines contains one of the described queries in the following format: " 1 p i " (1 ≤ p i < [ current width of sheet ]) — the first type query. " 2 l i r i " (0 ≤ l i < r i ≤ [ current width of sheet ]) — the second type query.
output_specification: For each query of the second type, output the answer.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 461C — Appleman and a Sheet of Paper [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
